title: Prisoner care problems highlighted before Sprague's death
article: Following the jail cell death of Adam Sprague, Cynthia Rayburn, chair of the Orangeville Police Services Board, didn't invest any thought into what transpired at the station that night.
"No, I did not," Rayburn told the Coroner's Inquest examining Sprague's death on Monday (May 5).
From her interpretation of the Police Services Act, the board is forbidden from getting involved in matters of operation within the Orangeville Police Service (OPS).
"We're not able to get involved in day to day operations," Rayburn said.
Sprague, who was arrested for public intoxication, died of an oxycodone overdose while in a holding cell at the C Line police station early in the morning of Nov. 11, 2010.
Karen Shea, council for the coroner, questioned how Sprague's death didn't trigger involvement from the board.
"This wasn't day to day activity, this was a death," Shea said.
However, Rayburn maintained the board is unable to get involved in police operations.
"Our responsibility is to bring board policies up," Rayburn said.

In 2008, the Ministry of Community Safety and Corrections made 22 recommendations to OPS following an inspection. Prisoner care and control was one of four areas of policing covered in the recommendations. Policies for prisoner care were not in compliance, according to the ministry.
"The ministry was very clear regular physical checks must take place for all prisoners," Shea said.

Police Chief Joe Tomei took interim measures and four special constables were hired to monitor jail cells, but OPS was still out of compliance, Shea explained. The board was eventually presented with a new policy on prisoner care in 2011.
Shea asked if the board was even shown another policy relating to prisoner care between 2008 and 2011.
"I didn't locate any policy," Rayburn said.
"Did the board not want to know the practice?" Shea asked.
"The board's hands are tied," Rayburn replied.
If the board isn't providing oversight of OPS, Shea asked who holds the responsibility. The ministry inspects the police station every three to five years.
"The ministry?" Rayburn said. "That would be part of their regular inspection."

While Rayburn maintained the board couldn't comment on police operations, Shea referenced two sets of recommendations that state otherwise, including a report prepared by judge John Morden following the G20 in Toronto.
Shea explained a board is allowed to ask questions.
"You had a responsibility to ask the chief questions," Shea said.
Elisabeth Widner, the lawyer representing Sprague's family, agreed the police board should have been asking about prisoner care and control.
"You failed to do that," Widner said.
The ministry had highlighted "serious risk management problem" within prisoner care, Widner explained.
"The board did nothing about that concern," Widner said. "You sat back and waited. You didn't take any steps."
Rayburn explained special constables were hired to watch prisoners in response to the ministry's recommendations, but said the board didn't know which direction to take.
"The Orangeville Police Service Board failed in its responsibility to its community," Widner replied.
Rayburn stressed the board did everything within its capability.
"I think we did the best job we could as a civilian board," Rayburn said.
"You didn't do anything," Widner replied.
Coroner Jack Stanborough asked Rayburn why she believed she received the Morden report.
"I believe it was for our information," Rayburn said.
Stanborough added the board is prevented from interfering with operations, but allowed to inquire into the service's day-to-day duties.
"It sounds like policy directs operations, policies are the rules. Operations carry out the rules," the coroner said.

Sgt. Chris Dryden, who holds standing at the inquest as the officer in charge the night of Sprague's death, asked Rayburn why the operations inspector at OPS was never replaced after retirement left the position open.
"We hired a deputy chief and a second staff sergeant,' Rayburn explained. "We still don't have an inspector."
Dryden told the inquest there were several years between the operations inspector's retirement and hiring a deputy chie
"No one filled that position for a number of years," Dryden said.
Rayburn explained she wasn't sure how much time had lapsed between hiring a deputy chief and the inspector's retirement.
"I'd have to look it up in a date calendar," she told the inquest.
"It sounds likes someone with oversight of operations is important," Stanborough said.

Rayburn became a member of the police service board in 2005 and was elected chair the following year. She holds a degree in art history and architecture and outside of the board works in landscaping. When she joined the board, Rayburn completed "four or five training" sessions and about one day of training per year since.
"There were quite a few when I first came on the board," she said.
Widner asked if Rayburn was even asked for her experience in policing or policy creation when applying to a position with the board.
"I don't' recall," Rayburn said. "I did work as a summer student on parliament."
While additional training is offered, Rayburn doesn't recall the opportunity to learn about legislation.
"Some have been too far for me to attend," Rayburn said.
In recent weeks, Rayburn said she spends about 10 hours a week in her role as chair of the board, about eight hours above the average. Widner asked if the spike in workload is due to the inquest.
"Yes, well no," Rayburn said. "We have things going on in our police service board."
